title: Adaptive evolution of a dominant plant species promotes spontaneous restoration of the plant community in a Pb–Zn mining area abandoned for 70 years
content:
Our study shows that, under heavy metal stress, highly tolerant plant species can rapidly colonize contaminated sites and achieve dominance. Through adaptive processes, these species undergo genetic differentiation and functional trait shifts that promote biomass recovery and stabilize community structure. These findings advance understanding of plant community assembly and persistence in extreme environments and provide a foundation for applying NBS to the ecological restoration of abandoned mining landscapes.

Abstract

Ecologists increasingly advocate for nature-based solutions (NBS) to mitigate pollution and ecosystem degradation in mining areas and to restore ecological functions. However, current restoration practices in mining regions often prioritize short-term environmental targets, overlooking the potential for natural recovery. Consequently, the mechanisms that sustain spontaneously colonized plant communities in mining areas remain poorly understood. We investigated a Pb–Zn mine abandoned for 70 years without human disturbance. Pollution sampling plots were established, and the dominant species, Artemisia lavandulifolia, was selected to assess the effects of chronic heavy metal contamination on intraspecific genetic diversity and to clarify how its adaptive evolution supports naturally assembled plant communities. Cadmium (Cd) was the primary biotoxic pollutant in the study area. A. lavandulifolia efficiently accumulated and translocated Cd, reducing local toxicity and facilitating the establishment of stress-tolerant species. Under long-term contamination, populations from polluted and control sites exhibited moderate genetic differentiation and reduced genetic diversity. Heavy metal stress also altered root morphology, decreasing mean root diameter, which enhanced alkaline phosphatase activity in the rhizosphere and alleviated phosphorus limitation. Elevated phosphorus levels in the soil further boosted below-ground community biomass, reinforcing the stability of spontaneously colonized plant communities. Synthesis and applications. Our study shows that, under heavy metal stress, highly tolerant plant species can rapidly colonize contaminated sites and achieve dominance. Through adaptive processes, these species undergo genetic differentiation and functional trait shifts that promote biomass recovery and stabilize community structure. These findings advance understanding of plant community assembly and persistence in extreme environments and provide a foundation for applying NBS to the ecological restoration of abandoned mining landscapes.
